claim: Animals excel at seamlessly integrating information from different senses, a capability critical for navigating complex environments.
source: Animals excel at seamlessly integrating information from different senses, a capability critical for navigating complex environments.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal sensory capabilities, drawing on established scientific knowledge about multisensory integration.

claim: The absence of stimulus-computable perceptual models fundamentally limits our understanding of how the brain extracts and combines task-relevant cues from the continuous flow of natural multisensory stimuli.
source: Despite recent progress in multisensory research, the absence of stimulus-computable perceptual models fundamentally limits our understanding of how the brain extracts and combines task-relevant cues from the continuous flow of natural multisensory stimuli.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current research methodology and is based on the authors' assessment of the field.

claim: The proposed model replicates human, monkey, and rat behaviour in response to diverse audiovisual stimuli with an average correlation exceeding 0.97.
source: In a large-scale simulation spanning 69 psychophysical, eye-tracking, and pharmacological experiments, our model replicates human, monkey, and rat behaviour in response to diverse audiovisual stimuli with an average correlation exceeding 0.97.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative results from simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model relies on as few as 0–4 free parameters.
source: Despite relying on as few as 0–4 free parameters, our model provides an end-to-end account of audiovisual integration in mammals—from individual pixels and audio samples to behavioural responses.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's parametric complexity, supported by the model specifications described in the Methods.

claim: The population response to natural audiovisual scenes generates saliency maps that predict spontaneous gaze direction.
source: Remarkably, the population response to natural audiovisual scenes generates saliency maps that predict spontaneous gaze direction, Bayesian causal inference, and a variety of previously reported multisensory illusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data comparisons shown in Figure 6.

claim: The integration of audiovisual stimuli can be accounted for in terms of elementary joint analyses of luminance and sound level.
source: This study demonstrates that the integration of audiovisual stimuli, regardless of their spatiotemporal complexity, can be accounted for in terms of elementary joint analyses of luminance and sound level.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's computational approach, supported by the simulations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The McGurk illusion demonstrates that the auditory perception of a syllable is altered by mismatched lip movements.
source: A compelling demonstration of this is the McGurk illusion (McGurk and MacDonald, 1976), where the auditory perception of a syllable is altered by mismatched lip movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original McGurk and MacDonald study.

claim: The ventriloquist illusion demonstrates that perceived sound location shifts toward a synchronous visual stimulus.
source: Likewise, audiovisual integration plays a critical role in spatial localization, as illustrated by the ventriloquist illusion (Stratton, 1897), where perceived sound location shifts toward a synchronous visual stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stratton's work on the ventriloquist illusion.

claim: Audiovisual integration occurs when visual and auditory stimuli are presented in close spatiotemporal proximity.
source: Extensive behavioural and neurophysiological findings demonstrate that audiovisual integration occurs when visual and auditory stimuli are presented in close spatiotemporal proximity (i.e. the spatial and temporal determinants of multisensory integration; Stein, 2012, Stein and Stanford, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stein's work on multisensory integration principles.

claim: When redundant multisensory information is integrated, the resulting percept is more reliable.
source: When redundant multisensory information is integrated, the resulting percept is more reliable (Ernst and Banks, 2002) and salient (Talsma et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ernst and Banks on reliability enhancement.

claim: When redundant multisensory information is integrated, the resulting percept is more salient.
source: When redundant multisensory information is integrated, the resulting percept is more reliable (Ernst and Banks, 2002) and salient (Talsma et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Talsma et al. on salience enhancement.

claim: Prevailing theoretical models of multisensory integration typically operate at the computational level as defined by Marr.
source: Prevailing theoretical models of multisensory integration typically operate at what Marr, 1982 termed the computational level: they describe what the system is trying to achieve (e.g. obtain precise sensory estimates).
evidence: This claim characterizes existing models using Marr's framework and is supported by a citation.

claim: Current multisensory integration models are not stimulus-computable.
source: However, these models are not stimulus-computable. That is, rather than analysing raw auditory and visual input directly, they rely on experimenter-defined, low-dimensional abstractions of the stimuli (Alais and Burr, 2004, Körding et al., 2007, Magnotti et al., 2013, Yarrow et al., 2023, Magnotti and Beauchamp, 2017)—such as the asynchrony between sound and image, expressed in seconds (Magnotti et al., 2013, Yarrow et al., 2023), or spatial location (Alais and Burr, 2004, Körding et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and describes a limitation of existing models.

claim: Current models solve a fundamentally different task than real perceptual systems, which must infer properties from the stimuli themselves without access to ground-truth parameters.
source: As a result, they solve a fundamentally different task than real perceptual systems, which must infer such properties from the stimuli themselves—from dynamic patterns of pixels and audio samples—without access to ground-truth parameters.
evidence: This is an inference about the difference between model behavior and biological perception.

claim: Current models remain silent on how perceptual systems extract, process, and combine task-relevant information from the continuous and structured stream of audiovisual signals.
source: Despite their clear success in accounting for behaviour in simple, controlled conditions, current models remain silent on how perceptual systems extract, process, and combine task-relevant information from the continuous and structured stream of audiovisual signals that real-world perception entails.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of current models based on their design.

claim: Currently, there are no stimulus-computable models for multisensory perception that can take as input natural audiovisual data, like movies.
source: Currently, there are no stimulus-computable models (Burge, 2020) for multisensory perception that can take as input natural audiovisual data, like movies.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by a citation to Burge.

claim: Moving lips generate patterns of light that vary in sync with the sound during audiovisual speech.
source: An instance of such a three-dimensional diagram for the case of audiovisual speech is shown in Figure 1B (top): moving lips generate patterns of light that vary in sync with the sound.
evidence: This claim describes a property of audiovisual speech stimuli and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Audiovisual correspondence can be detected by a local correlator that operates across space, time, and the senses.
source: In such a representation, audiovisual correspondence can be detected by a local correlator (i.e. multiplier), that operates across space, time, and the senses (Parise et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim proposes a computational mechanism and is supported by a citation.

claim: The model provides a comprehensive bottom-up account for multisensory integration in mammals, encompassing its temporal, spatial, and attentional aspects.
source: Here, we will illustrate how a population of multisensory correlation detectors can take real-life footage as input and provide a comprehensive bottom-up account for multisensory integration in mammals, encompassing its temporal, spatial, and attentional aspects.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's capabilities, supported by the simulations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The model provided a good fit to the empirical psychometric functions with an average Pearson correlation of 0.981 for humans.
source: Overall, the model provided a good fit to the empirical psychometric functions, and the average Pearson correlation between human and model response (weighted by sample size) is 0.981 for humans and 0.994 for rats.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulations.

claim: The model provided a good fit to the empirical psychometric functions with an average Pearson correlation of 0.994 for rats.
source: Overall, the model provided a good fit to the empirical psychometric functions, and the average Pearson correlation between human and model response (weighted by sample size) is 0.981 for humans and 0.994 for rats.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulations.

claim: The psychometric curves predicted from matching stimuli provided a significantly better fit than mismatching stimuli (p<0.001).
source: The psychometric curves predicted from the matching stimuli provided a significantly better fit than mismatching stimuli (p<0.001, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is a statistical result from a permutation test, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The model captures the subtle effects of how individual features affect observed responses.
source: This demonstrates that our model captures the subtle effects of how individual features affect observed responses, and it highlights the role of low-level stimulus properties on multisensory perception.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the permutation test results.

claim: Humans scale subjective audiovisual synchrony with distance to compensate for different propagation speeds of light and sound.
source: Psychophysical temporal order judgments demonstrate that, to compensate for these lags, humans scale subjective audiovisual synchrony with distance (Figure 2B; Alais and Carlile, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alais and Carlile and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Humans exploit auditory spatial cues, such as the direct-to-reverberant energy ratio, to estimate the distance of the sound source.
source: This result has been interpreted as evidence that humans exploit auditory spatial cues, such as the direct-to-reverberant energy ratio (Figure 2B, left), to estimate the distance of the sound source and adjust subjective synchrony by scaling distance estimates by the speed of sound (Alais and Carlile, 2005).
evidence: This claim describes an interpretation from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The model predicts the observed shifts in subjective simultaneity with distance without relying on explicit spatial representations and physics simulations.
source: When presented with the same stimuli, our model also predicts the observed shifts in subjective simultaneity (Figure 2B, centre). However, rather than relying on explicit spatial representations and physics simulations, these shifts emerge from elementary analyses of natural audiovisual signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In reverberant environments, the intensity of the direct portion of a sound increases with source proximity, while the reverberant component remains constant.
source: Specifically, in reverberant environments, the intensity of the direct portion of a sound increases with source proximity, while the reverberant component remains constant.
evidence: This is a statement about acoustic properties in reverberant environments, based on established knowledge.

claim: The envelopes of sounds originating close to observers are more front-heavy than distant sounds in reverberant environments.
source: As a result, the envelopes of sounds originating close to the observers are more front-heavy than distant sounds (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: This is an inference about acoustic signal properties, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The model could tightly replicate rats' behaviour with a correlation of 0.981.
source: Overall, we could tightly replicate rats' behaviour (rho = 0.981; see Figure 2C-E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), including the effect of loudness on observed responses (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulations of rat behavior.

claim: The unimodal temporal constants for rats were 4 times faster than for humans.
source: Interestingly, the unimodal temporal constants for rats were 4 times faster than for humans: such a different temporal tuning is reflected in higher sensitivity in rats for short lags (<0.1 s), and in humans for longer lags (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from parameter estimation and model comparison.

claim: The fourfold difference in temporal tuning between rats and humans closely mirrors analogous interspecies differences in physiological rhythms, such as heart rate (~4.7 times faster in rats) and breathing rate (~6.3 times faster in rats).
source: This fourfold difference in temporal tuning between rats and humans closely mirrors analogous interspecies differences in physiological rhythms, such as heart rate (~4.7 times faster in rats) and breathing rate (~6.3 times faster in rats) (Agoston, 2017).
evidence: This claim compares model parameters to physiological data, supported by a citation.

claim: Pharmacologically-induced changes in audiovisual time perception in rats could be accounted for solely by changes in the decision-making process.
source: While tuning the temporal constants of the model was necessary to account for the difference between humans and rats, this was not necessary to reproduce pharmacologically-induced changes in audiovisual time perception in rats (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-G), which could be accounted for solely by changes in the decision-making process(Equation 10).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations of pharmacological manipulations.

claim: The observed pharmacological effects can be explained without altering low-level temporal processing.
source: This suggests that the observed effects can be explained without altering low-level temporal processing. However, this does not imply that such changes did not occur—only that they were not required to reproduce the behavioural data in our simulations.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the model results.

claim: Model responses cluster mostly around the mouth area and (to a lesser extent) the eyes during audiovisual speech.
source: This is illustrated in Figure 3 and Videos 1 and 2 for the case of audiovisual speech, where model responses cluster mostly around the mouth area and (to a lesser extent) the eyes.
evidence: This is a description of model output shown in Figure 3 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The regions where model responses cluster are the regions where pixels' luminance changes in synch with the audio track.
source: These are the regions where pixels' luminance changes in synch with the audio track.
evidence: This is an explanation of why the model responds in certain regions, based on the model's computational principles.

claim: The time-averaged MCD population response is equivalent to MLE.
source: Given that both the MLE and the MCD operate by multiplying unimodal inputs (see Methods), the time-averaged MCD population response (Equation 16) is equivalent to MLE (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the relationship between the MCD and MLE models, demonstrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The integrated percept predicted by the MCD and MLE models is statistically indistinguishable.
source: Figure 4C shows that the integrated percept predicted by the two models is statistically indistinguishable.
evidence: This is a result from comparing the two models, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A population of MCDs can jointly account for the observed bias and precision of the bimodal percept with zero parameters.
source: As such, a population of MCDs (Equation 16) can jointly account for the observed bias and precision of the bimodal percept (Figure 4D–E), with zero parameters.
evidence: This is a result from simulating the Alais and Burr experiment, shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Integration eventually breaks down with increasing spatial disparity across the senses.
source: While fusing audiovisual cues is a sensible solution in the presence of minor spatial discrepancies across the senses, integration eventually breaks down with increasing disparity (Chen and Vroomen, 2013)—when the spatial (or temporal) conflict is too large, visual and auditory signals may well be unrelated.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Vroomen.

claim: The Bayesian Causal Inference model weighs uni- and bimodal location estimates based on the probability that the two modalities share a common cause.
source: To account for the breakdown of multisensory integration in the presence of intersensory conflicts, Körding and colleagues proposed the influential Bayesian Causal Inference (BCI) model (Körding et al., 2007), where uni- and bimodal location estimates are weighted based on the probability that the two modalities share a common cause (Equation 17).
evidence: This describes the BCI model and is supported by a citation to Körding et al.

claim: Visual and auditory stimuli preferentially bias each other when the discrepancy is low, with the bias progressively declining as the discrepancy increases.
source: Results demonstrate that visual and auditory stimuli preferentially bias each other when the discrepancy is low, with the bias progressively declining as the discrepancy increases.
evidence: This describes a finding from the Körding et al. experiment.

claim: A population of MCDs can compute the probability that auditory and visual stimuli share a common cause.
source: Also a population of MCDs can compute the probability that auditory and visual stimuli share a common cause (Figure 1B and D; Figure 4F, Equation 19), therefore, we can test whether it can also implement BCI.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the MCD model's capabilities, illustrated in figures.

claim: The MCD model near-perfectly replicated the empirical data from Körding et al. with a correlation of 0.99.
source: For that, we simulated the experiment of Körding and colleagues, and fed the stimuli to a population of MCDs (Equations 18-20) which near-perfectly replicated the empirical data (rho = 0.99)–even slightly outperforming the BCI model.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulating the Körding et al. experiment.

claim: If observers infer a common cause, they tend to make a single fixation; otherwise, two—one for each modality.
source: If observers infer a common cause, they tend to make a single fixation; otherwise, two—one for each modality.
evidence: This describes the behavioral pattern observed in the Mohl et al. experiment.

claim: The probability of a single fixation decreased with increasing disparity.
source: As expected, the probability of a single fixation decreased with increasing disparity (Figure 4H, right).
evidence: This is a result from the Mohl et al. experiment, shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The model was able to predict the full distribution of gaze locations in both humans and monkeys with zero additional free parameters.
source: Critically, using this fit, the model was then able to predict the full distribution of gaze locations (Equation 20, Figure 4H, left) in both species with zero additional free parameters.
evidence: This is a result from simulating the Mohl et al. experiment.

claim: Behaviour consistent with BCI and MLE naturally emerges from a population of MCDs.
source: Taken together, these simulations show that behaviour consistent with BCI and MLE naturally emerges from a population of MCDs.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the spatial integration simulations.

claim: The MCD population model is both image- and sound-computable.
source: Unlike BCI and MLE, however, the MCD population model is both image- and sound-computable, and it explicitly represents the spatiotemporal dynamics of the process (Figure 4A, bottom; Figure 3B; Figure 5; Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's capabilities, illustrated in multiple figures.

claim: The MCD model enables application to complex, dynamic audiovisual stimuli that were previously off limits to traditional BCI and MLE frameworks.
source: By operating directly on realistic audiovisual signals, our population model captures the richness of natural sensory input and directly addresses the problem of how biological systems represent and process multisensory information (Burge, 2020). This allows the MCD to generate precise, stimulus-specific predictions across tasks, including subtle differences in behavioural outcomes that arise from the structure of individual stimuli (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the MCD approach, supported by citation and data.

claim: The model permits direct, time-resolved comparisons between model responses and neurophysiological measures.
source: On the other, it permits direct, time-resolved comparisons between model responses and neurophysiological measures (Pesnot Lerousseau et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous neurophysiological study.

claim: The population response dynamically tracked the active talker in a video of a performing ventriloquist.
source: As a practical demonstration, we applied the model (Equation 6) to a real-life video of a performing ventriloquist (Figure 5). The population response dynamically tracked the active talker, clustering around the dummy's face whenever it produced speech Video 3.
evidence: This is a result from applying the model to a ventriloquist video, shown in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claim: Multisensory stimuli are typically salient.
source: Multisensory stimuli are typically salient, and a vast body of literature demonstrates that spatial attention is commonly attracted to audiovisual stimuli (Talsma et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Talsma et al.

claim: Spatial attention is commonly attracted to audiovisual stimuli.
source: Multisensory stimuli are typically salient, and a vast body of literature demonstrates that spatial attention is commonly attracted to audiovisual stimuli (Talsma et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Talsma et al.

claim: The dynamic MCD response explicitly represents the regions in space with the highest audiovisual correspondence for each point in time.
source: This aspect of multisensory perception is naturally captured by a population of MCDs, whose dynamic response explicitly represents the regions in space with the highest audiovisual correspondence for each point in time.
evidence: This is a description of the model's output properties.

claim: Elementary audiovisual analyses are sufficient to replicate behaviours consistent with multisensory perception in mammals.
source: This study demonstrates that elementary audiovisual analyses are sufficient to replicate behaviours consistent with multisensory perception in mammals.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the study's main finding.

claim: The model closely matched observed behaviour across a wide range of phenomena with average correlations above 0.97.
source: Starting directly from pixels and audio samples, our model closely matched observed behaviour across a wide range of phenomena—including multisensory illusions, spatial orienting, and causal inference—with average correlations above 0.97.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative results across all simulations.

claim: The model was tested in a large-scale simulation spanning 69 audiovisual experiments, seven behavioural tasks, and data from 534 humans, 110 rats, and two monkeys.
source: This was tested in a large-scale simulation spanning 69 audiovisual experiments, seven behavioural tasks, and data from 534 humans, 110 rats, and two monkeys.
evidence: This describes the scope of the simulations performed in the study.

claim: Stimulus-computable models operate at the algorithmic level, specifying how sensory information is represented and processed.
source: Framed in Marr's terms, stimulus-computable models operate at the algorithmic level, specifying how sensory information is represented and processed.
evidence: This is a theoretical characterization using Marr's framework.

claim: The MCD provides a mechanistic substrate that could plausibly implement Bayesian ideal observer models.
source: Rather than competing with such normative accounts, the MCD provides a mechanistic substrate that could plausibly implement them.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the relationship between the MCD and normative models.

claim: The MCD can generate precise, stimulus-specific predictions across tasks, including subtle differences in behavioural outcomes that arise from the structure of individual stimuli.
source: This allows the MCD to generate precise, stimulus-specific predictions across tasks, including subtle differences in behavioural outcomes that arise from the structure of individual stimuli (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by the permutation test results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Auditory cues embedded in the envelope are sufficient to scale subjective audiovisual synchrony with distance.
source: Although this phenomenon appears to rely on explicit physics modelling, our simulations demonstrate that auditory cues embedded in the envelope (Figure 2B, left) are sufficient to scale subjective audiovisual synchrony.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation of the Alais and Carlile experiment.

claim: Phenomena such as the McGurk illusion and the subjective timing of natural audiovisual stimuli may emerge from elementary operations performed at pixel level.
source: In a similar fashion, our simulations show that phenomena such as the McGurk illusion, the subjective timing of natural audiovisual stimuli, and saliency detection may emerge from elementary operations performed at pixel level, bypassing the need for more sophisticated analyses such as image segmentation, lip or face tracking, 3D reconstruction, etc (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the model's performance, supported by a citation.

claim: Elementary, general-purpose operations on natural stimuli can drive complex behaviour, sometimes even in the absence of advanced perceptual and cognitive contributions.
source: Elementary, general-purpose operations on natural stimuli can drive complex behaviour, sometimes even in the absence of advanced perceptual and cognitive contributions.
evidence: This is a general inference from the study's findings.

claim: Identical low-level analyses can account for all of the 69 experiments simulated in the study.
source: The fact that identical low-level analyses can account for all of the 69 experiments simulated here directly addresses several open questions in multisensory research.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the model's generality.

claim: Psychometric functions for speech and non-speech stimuli often differ significantly.
source: For instance, psychometric functions for speech and non-speech stimuli often differ significantly (Vatakis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vatakis et al.

claim: Speech may be special and processed via dedicated mechanisms.
source: This has been interpreted as evidence that speech may be special and processed via dedicated mechanisms (Tuomainen et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes an interpretation from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Most of the differences in psychometric curves across classes of stimuli are due to the low-level features of the stimuli themselves, not how the brain processes them.
source: This suggests that most of the differences in psychometric curves across classes of stimuli (e.g. speech vs. non-speech vs. clicks-&-flashes) are due to the low-level features of the stimuli themselves, not how the brain processes them.
evidence: This is an inference from the model's ability to account for different stimulus types with the same parameters.

claim: Audiovisual simultaneity judgments differ significantly between musicians and non-musicians.
source: For example, audiovisual simultaneity judgments differ significantly between musicians and non-musicians (Lee and Noppeney, 2011) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The McGurk illusion and subjective audiovisual timing vary over the lifespan in humans.
source: Likewise, the McGurk illusion (Freeman et al., 2013) and subjective audiovisual timing (Petrini et al., 2009) vary over the lifespan in humans, and following pharmacological interventions in rats (Al Youzbaki et al., 2023; Schormans and Allman, 2023) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in supplementary figures.

claim: Adjustments at the decision-making level are sufficient to account for effects of experience, expertise, and pharmacological interventions, without requiring structural or parametric changes to low-level perceptual processing.
source: Our simulations show that adjustments at the decision-making level are sufficient to account for these effects, without requiring structural or parametric changes to low-level perceptual processing across observers or conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claim: The temporal constants vary across species (humans, rats, and monkeys).
source: Although the same model explains responses to multisensory stimuli in humans, rats, and monkeys, the temporal constants vary across species.
evidence: This is a finding from parameter estimation across species.

claim: The model for rats is tuned to temporal frequencies over four times higher than those for humans.
source: For example, the model for rats is tuned to temporal frequencies over four times higher than those for humans.
evidence: This is a finding from parameter estimation.

claim: The differential sensitivity of humans and rats to long and short audiovisual lags mirrors analogous interspecies differences in physiological rhythms.
source: This not only explains the differential sensitivity of humans and rats to long and short audiovisual lags, but it also mirrors analogous interspecies differences in physiological rhythms, such as heart and breathing rates (Agoston, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference connecting model parameters to physiological data, supported by a citation.

claim: Physiological arousal modulates perceptual rhythms within individuals.
source: Previous research has shown that physiological arousal modulates perceptual rhythms within individuals (Legrand et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Legrand et al.

claim: No major differences in the model's spatial tuning were found between humans and macaques.
source: Conversely, no major differences in the model's spatial tuning were found between humans and macaques, possibly reflecting the close phylogenetic link between the two species.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial integration simulations.

claim: Neural responses in the posterior superior temporal sulcus, superior temporal gyrus, and left superior parietal gyrus tracked the output of an MCD model during audiovisual temporal tasks.
source: In a recent study (Pesnot Lerousseau et al., 2022), we identified neural responses in the posterior superior temporal sulcus, superior temporal gyrus, and left superior parietal gyrus that tracked the output of an MCD model during audiovisual temporal tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous neurophysiological study.

claim: MCD dynamics aligned closely with stimulus-evoked cortical activity.
source: By applying a time-resolved encoding model to MEG data, we demonstrated that MCD dynamics aligned closely with stimulus-evoked cortical activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous MEG study.

claim: The model's ability to predict spontaneous gaze direction in response to naturalistic audiovisual stimuli is an informative outcome.
source: An informative outcome of our simulations is the model's ability to predict spontaneous gaze direction in response to naturalistic audiovisual stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the eye-tracking results.

claim: Current audiovisual saliency models are often computationally expensive.
source: Despite successfully predicting gaze behaviour, current audiovisual saliency models are often computationally expensive, and the resulting maps are hard to interpret and inevitably affected by the datasets used for training (Adebayo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Adebayo et al.

claim: The MCD model detects saliency 'out of the box,' without any free parameters.
source: In contrast, our model detects saliency 'out of the box,' without any free parameters, and operating purely at the individual pixel level.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's capabilities.

claim: Salient points are those with high audiovisual correlation.
source: The elementary nature of the operations performed by a population of MCDs returns saliency maps that are easy to interpret: salient points are those with high audiovisual correlation.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the model defines saliency.

claim: The framework provides a solution for self-supervised and unsupervised audiovisual learning in multimodal machine perception.
source: This framework also provides a solution for self-supervised and unsupervised audiovisual learning in multimodal machine perception.
evidence: This is a claim about potential applications of the model.

claim: A biomimetic module that handles saliency maps, audiovisual correspondence detection, and multimodal fusion can drive self-supervised learning through simulated observers.
source: In this context, a biomimetic module that handles saliency maps, audiovisual correspondence detection, and multimodal fusion can drive self-supervised learning through simulated observers, thereby reducing the dependency on labelled data (Shahabaz and Sarkar, 2024; Arandjelovic and Zisserman, 2017; Ngiam et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claim: The simplicity of the population-based model provides a computationally efficient alternative for real-time multisensory integration in applications such as robotics, AR/VR, and other low-latency systems.
source: Furthermore, the simplicity of our population-based model provides a computationally efficient alternative for real-time multisensory integration in applications such as robotics, AR/VR, and other low-latency systems.
evidence: This is a claim about potential applications of the model.

claim: A population of MCDs can explain when phenomena such as the McGurk Illusion occur, but it does not explain the process of phoneme categorization.
source: Although a population of MCDs can explain when phenomena such as the McGurk Illusion occur, it does not explain the process of phoneme categorization that ultimately determines what syllable is perceived (Magnotti and Beauchamp, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the model, supported by a citation.

claim: Cognitive and affective factors modulate our responses to multisensory stimuli.
source: More generally, it is well known that cognitive and affective factors modulate our responses to multisensory stimuli (Stein, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stein.

claim: The model does not currently incorporate linguistic mechanisms or top-down predictive processes.
source: In particular, the model does not currently incorporate linguistic mechanisms or top-down predictive processes, which play a central role in audiovisual speech perception—such as the integration of complementary articulatory features, lexical expectations, or syntactic constraints (Campbell, 2008; Peelle and Sommers, 2015; Summerfield, 1987; Tye-Murray et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's limitations, supported by citations.

claim: The modularity of the approach makes it possible to extend the system to include high-level perceptual, cognitive, and affective factors.
source: While a purely low-level model does not directly address these issues, the modularity of our approach makes it possible to extend the system to include high-level perceptual, cognitive, and affective factors.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential extensibility of the model.

claim: The same approach can be naturally extended to other instances of sensory integration (e.g. visuo- and audio-tactile) and animal classes.
source: What is more, although this study focused on audiovisual integration in mammals, the same approach can be naturally extended to other instances of sensory integration (e.g. visuo- and audio-tactile) and animal classes.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential generalizability of the approach.

claim: A stimulus-computable approach makes explicit all the intermediate steps of sensory information processing.
source: Besides simulating behavioural responses, a stimulus-computable approach necessarily makes explicit all the intermediate steps of sensory information processing.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the stimulus-computable approach.

claim: The transparency of the Hassenstein-Reichardt detector made it possible to link computation, behavior, and physiology at the scale of individual cells in insect motion vision.
source: In insect motion vision, this transparency made it possible for the Hassenstein-Reichardt detector to act as a searchlight to link computation, behavior, and physiology at the scale of individual cells (Serbe et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Serbe et al.

claim: The present approach holds the same potential for multisensory perception as the Hassenstein-Reichardt detector did for insect motion vision.
source: Being based on formally identical computational principles (Parise and Ernst, 2016), the present approach holds the same potential for multisensory perception.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential impact of the approach, supported by a citation.
